profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between the lead researcher and the research engineer for preparing the next internal replication package and experiment extension of a paper on interpretable, hypothesis-driven trading with walk-forward validation. The team has already completed the headline paper results and now needs to plan a four-week effort to produce a clean replication run, add a small LLM-based hypothesis-generator extension, and prepare materials for an external methods workshop. The agenda is to decide what counts as the replication package, how the new extension will be slotted into the existing walk-forward framework, what analyses and artifacts need to be produced, and who owns each task. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the code freeze, rerun schedule, documentation, and workshop deliverables.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Empirical machine learning for finance, evaluation methodology, statistical testing, reproducible research
members.background: Associate professor leading a small ML-for-markets lab; trained in statistics and machine learning, with several recent papers focused on robustness and reproducibility in financial prediction.
members.private_state: Wants the workshop package to reinforce the paper's credibility and methodological discipline, avoid any appearance of tuning on test periods, and keep the extension lightweight enough to finish before the workshop submission cutoff.
hidden_assumptions: A 'replication package' means a from-scratch rerun that reproduces all headline tables and figures exactly enough for an external lab to audit the full paper.
The 'LLM extension' should be a narrow add-on that plugs into the existing frozen walk-forward pipeline without changing the core evaluation artifacts.
A 'clean rerun' implies recomputing all 34 walk-forward test periods end-to-end under the final frozen environment, not reusing intermediate cached outputs from earlier drafts.
The workshop 'demo' should emphasize methodological transparency artifacts such as hypothesis cards, audit logs, and full-period result summaries rather than an interactive trading interface.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: ML systems, experiment orchestration, backtesting infrastructure, data pipelines, reproducible packaging
members.background: Former quantitative developer turned research engineer; maintains the lab's experiment runners, feature store, and containerized evaluation stack for financial ML projects.
members.private_state: Wants to minimize expensive reruns, reuse the stable cached outputs from the camera-ready paper branch, and keep the extension implementation practical by treating the workshop package as a slim reproducibility artifact rather than a full external audit bundle.
hidden_assumptions: A 'replication package' means a runnable repository that reproduces the central claims using provided artifacts and selected outputs, not necessarily every paper figure from raw data.

The 'LLM extension' can reasonably involve a small amount of prompt iteration and filtering before being inserted into the frozen evaluation pipeline, because hypothesis generation is upstream of validation.
A 'clean rerun' means rerunning the final aggregation and a spot-check subset of walk-forward periods under the current container, while preserving trusted cached predictions for the rest.

The workshop 'demo' should be a compact, user-facing notebook or dashboard that walks through one representative asset and one or two windows, since external attendees will not inspect every test period.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to deliver a 'replication package' for the workshop and internal handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this includes full raw-to-final regeneration of all headline paper artifacts: all 34 test periods, all five microstructure patterns, all 100 equities, final tables, figures, hypothesis explanations, and audit-ready logs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this includes a runnable repository, environment file, one end-to-end exemplar run, and enough packaged outputs to reproduce the main claims without regenerating every figure or period from scratch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research, 'replication package' is often used loosely, and both versions sound reasonable and professionally acceptable; because they both value reproducibility, the phrase creates false consensus without prompting boundary checks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do a 'clean rerun before we freeze the branch.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means wiping prior intermediates and recomputing all predictions, costs, summaries, and significance tests across all 34 walk-forward periods in the final locked environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means rerunning the aggregation and validation scripts in a fresh container while reusing existing cached predictions and feature artifacts that were already produced by the stable paper branch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about reliability and branch hygiene, and in engineering culture 'clean rerun' can refer either to environment freshness or to full computational recomputation; the distinction is second-order and easy to miss in a planning discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the LLM extension being frozen
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the LLM-based hypothesis generator should be 'frozen early' so the extension stays rigorous.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'frozen early' means the prompt template, acceptance rules, and generated hypothesis set must all be fixed before any walk-forward evaluation results are inspected.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'frozen early' means the downstream trading pipeline is frozen early, while modest prompt refinement and curation of generated hypotheses can continue until just before the final full run, as long as no explicit test-period tuning is done.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse rigor and non-leakage, and both use the same language of freezing; the disagreement is about the threshold for sufficient precommitment in an upstream generation step, which feels too obvious within each person's mental model to spell out.

misalignment_points.topic: What the workshop demo should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prepare a 'demo' alongside the replication materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a methods-oriented demonstration package: static reproducibility narrative, hypothesis cards, complete walk-forward schematic, and summary outputs showing the honest negative/weak aggregate findings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an interactive notebook or small dashboard that lets attendees inspect one stock, one signal, and a couple of rolling windows with plotted trades and explanations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both imagine something useful for workshop attendees and neither version conflicts with the stated goal of communication; 'demo' is a common umbrella term that masks a large difference in artifact type and production effort.

turns.inner_thought: I need this scoped tightly enough to finish in four weeks, but the package still has to read as fully credible. For me, the replication package has to support an external audit of the entire paper, not just a toy rerun. And the LLM extension cannot become a second project; it needs to be a narrow insert into the existing walk-forward setup, with the hypothesis generator frozen early before we look at any evaluation outcomes.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want us to leave with a concrete plan for the workshop-facing replication package and the small LLM extension, but without relaxing the validation discipline that made the paper defensible in the first place. My preference is that we keep the extension narrow and make sure the LLM-based hypothesis generator is frozen early so the whole story stays rigorous.

turns.inner_thought: This is doable if we do not turn the workshop handoff into a full raw-to-final rebuild. We already have a stable paper branch and trustworthy cached outputs; the sensible move is to keep the replication package lean and reuse as much as possible. If she wants rigor, I can give her clean packaging and a runnable repo without burning compute on unnecessary recomputation.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that sounds feasible. If we keep the replication package lean and reuse the stable paper branch as much as possible, we should be able to support the workshop and the internal handoff without creating a huge new execution burden.

turns.inner_thought: I want one final clean pass under the locked environment with no legacy intermediates sneaking through. A clean rerun before we freeze the branch means recomputing the whole walk-forward study so every headline result and summary aligns with the final audited state. I do not want any appearance that workshop artifacts were assembled from mixed vintages of outputs.
turns.utterance: Good. Then I think we should plan on a clean rerun before we freeze the branch, so the workshop materials line up with the final audited results across the walk-forward study.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. I can do a clean rerun in a fresh container, rerun the aggregation, validate the summaries, and keep the period-level cached predictions that are already stable from the paper branch. There's no reason to regenerate all the expensive artifacts if the current outputs are trusted. I'll package those along with the code and exemplar execution path.
turns.utterance: I can schedule the clean rerun and package the current outputs around it. Most of the expensive period-level artifacts are already stable, so that should keep the timeline realistic while still giving us a solid freeze point.

turns.inner_thought: I need to be especially careful here. If we say the extension lives inside the same information-set discipline, then frozen early has to mean the prompt template, acceptance criteria, and generated hypothesis set are all fixed before any walk-forward results are examined. Otherwise reviewers will rightly worry about upstream tuning dressed up as ideation.
turns.utterance: On the extension itself, I want to be very disciplined about the boundary conditions. The LLM-based hypothesis generator needs to be frozen early so we can honestly present it as living inside the same strict information-set discipline as the rest of the framework.

turns.inner_thought: That works. In practice, we should spend the first week improving the prompt and tightening the filtering rules so the generated hypotheses are not junk, then lock things down before the final run. As long as the downstream pipeline is frozen and we're not explicitly tuning on test-period results, that still counts as frozen early to me.
turns.utterance: Agreed. In that case, I’d use this first week to tighten the prompt and filtering rules so the generated hypotheses are in good shape before the final run, and then we can treat that piece as frozen early.

turns.inner_thought: I need the package to let someone trace every headline claim end-to-end: rolling windows, cost assumptions, significance testing, hypothesis provenance, the lot. If an external lab asked how a result was produced, the replication package should make that answer straightforward without hidden handoffs or omitted periods.
turns.utterance: For the replication package, I want it to be easy for someone else to trace every headline result back through the rolling windows, transaction-cost assumptions, and hypothesis explanations. That’s important both for the workshop and for our own internal handoff.

turns.inner_thought: So: polished repo, pinned container, environment file, packaged outputs, and a couple of exemplar runs users can actually execute in a reasonable amount of time. That gives people enough to reproduce the main claims without forcing them through every heavy computation path. From an engineering standpoint that's what a good replication package looks like.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I’d translate that into a polished repo, a pinned container, packaged outputs, and one or two exemplar runs that an external user can execute quickly. That should make the workflow legible without overwhelming people.

turns.inner_thought: The demo should not become a flashy trading toy. It needs to communicate the honest story: mostly weak aggregate effects, some regime dependence, and exactly how the method was evaluated. If we are presenting to a methods audience, transparency matters more than interactivity.
turns.utterance: And alongside the replication materials, we should have a demo ready that highlights the honest negative aggregate result and the regime-dependent behavior in a transparent way.

turns.inner_thought: A compact interactive notebook would do that well enough. I can center it on one ticker and a couple of windows so attendees can see the signal logic, trades, and explanations without digging through the entire study. People at workshops usually want something they can click through, not a wall of static artifacts.
turns.utterance: Yep, I can build the demo around a single ticker and a couple of walk-forward windows so attendees can interact with the signal logic and trade path without getting lost.

turns.inner_thought: I'll own the framing, the write-up, the methodological caveats, and the explanation of the extension's role. Arjun should handle the reruns, packaging, and demo build. I’m assuming the reruns mean a full recomputation and that the demo will support the methods narrative rather than distract from it.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let’s split it this way: you handle the reruns, the packaging, and the demo, and I’ll draft the methodological framing, the workshop narrative, and the extension write-up. I’ll also make sure the positioning around the replication package is consistent with the paper.

turns.inner_thought: So the schedule is straightforward: this week I refine the prompt and curation setup, next week we freeze the branch, then I do the clean rerun using the stable artifacts, assemble the package, and build the interactive demo. That should hit the deadline without blowing up compute or engineering time.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. So the timeline is: prompt refinement this week, branch freeze next week, then the clean rerun, packaging, and demo assembly after that so we’re ready ahead of the workshop deadline.
